ukmt-sk-2017-01.title: Two alternating values
ukmt-sk-2017-01.body:
Every circle on the network holds one of two values: if all segment sums equal $S$, every neighbour of a circle holding $v$ holds $S-v$, and the network is connected and bipartite. So one class of circles holds $4$ and the other class holds some number $x$ with $4+x=S$; the circle marked $7$ is in the second class, so $x=7$. There are $12$ circles of each class, so the total is $12\times4+12\times7=132$.

**Answer: 132**

ukmt-sk-2017-02.title: Parity of swaps
ukmt-sk-2017-02.body:
A pair that changes places an even number of times ends in its starting order; an odd number of times, in the opposite order. Start: $1,2,3$ in order. Pair $(1,2)$ swaps $9$ times (odd): $2$ finishes ahead of $1$. Pair $(2,3)$ swaps $10$ times (even): $2$ ahead of $3$. Pair $(1,3)$ swaps $11$ times (odd): $3$ ahead of $1$. So the finishing order is $2,3,1$.

**Answer: 231**

ukmt-sk-2017-04.title: Angles at a vertex of the hexagon
ukmt-sk-2017-04.body:
Each square has side $18$, so each triangle has two sides of $18$. At a vertex of the hexagon the angles are $120^\circ$ (hexagon), $90^\circ$ and $90^\circ$ (two squares) and the triangle's apex angle $x$: $x+300=360$, so $x=60^\circ$ and each triangle is equilateral with side $18$. The outer boundary has $12$ edges of length $18$: $P=12\times18=216$.

**Answer: 216**

ukmt-sk-2017-05.title: Rotate the triangle
ukmt-sk-2017-05.body:
Draw the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$ and let it meet $BC$ extended at $F$. Triangles $ADE$ and $CDF$ are congruent (both right-angled, $AD=CD$, and $\angle ADE=\angle CDF$ since each is $90^\circ-\angle EDC$). So $DF=DE=25$, and the area of $ABCD$ equals the area of square $DEBF$ (the triangle $ADE$ is replaced by $CDF$): $25\times25=625$.

**Answer: 625**

ukmt-sk-2017-06.title: Count step by step
ukmt-sk-2017-06.body:
Multiples of $3$: $\lfloor2017/3\rfloor=672$, leaving $1345$. Multiples of $6$: $336$ reinstated, giving $1681$. The only multiples of $27$ on the board then are multiples of $6$, i.e. multiples of $54$: $\lfloor2017/54\rfloor=37$ are erased, leaving $1644$. Missing: $2017-1644=373$.

**Answer: 373**

ukmt-sk-2017-07.title: Enumerate the layouts
ukmt-sk-2017-07.body:
The two given rectangles share no side length, so they cannot be placed side by side in a row of three; they cannot be the stacked pair either. So the layout is: one rectangle $A$ of full height $H$, next to a stack of the other given rectangle $B$ and the third rectangle $X$, which have the same width $u$.

- $A=70\times110$ with $H=110$: $B$ with $(u,h)=(40,80)$ gives $X=40\times30$ (perimeter $140$); $B$ with $(u,h)=(80,40)$ gives $X=80\times70$ (perimeter $300$).
- $A=70\times110$ with $H=70$: $B$ with $(u,h)=(80,40)$ gives $X=80\times30$ (perimeter $220$).
- $A=40\times80$ with $H=80$: $B$ with $(u,h)=(110,70)$ gives $X=110\times10$ (perimeter $240$).

The other orientations do not fit. The maximum perimeter is $300$.

**Answer: 300**

ukmt-sk-2017-08.title: Angles of the hands
ukmt-sk-2017-08.body:
Let $s$ be the seconds since midday and $x$ the angle of each hand from the vertical. The hour hand turns $30^\circ$ per hour, i.e. $1^\circ$ per $120$ s: $s=120x$. The minute hand turns $360^\circ$ per hour, i.e. $1^\circ$ per $10$ s, and it has turned clockwise through $360-x$ degrees (it is $x$ short of a full turn): $s=10(360-x)$. Equating: $120x=3600-10x$, $x=\frac{360}{13}$ and $s=\frac{43200}{13}=3323\frac1{13}$. The time left in the hour is $3600-3323\frac1{13}\approx276.9$ s, so $276$ whole seconds remain.

**Answer: 276**

ukmt-sk-2017-09.title: List the possible totals
ukmt-sk-2017-09.body:
Zero is possible (miss, or adjacent regions). Otherwise all three arrows hit pairwise non-adjacent regions; arrows may land in the same region. The regions $7,1,3,5$ form a ring around the centre ($11$) and the outside region ($9$), so non-adjacent combinations are: all in one region (totals $3,9,15,21,27,33$ from $1,3,5,7,9,11$), or two different non-adjacent regions: $\{1,5\}$ (opposite quadrants): $7,11$; $\{7,3\}$: $13,17$; $\{9,11\}$: $29,31$. The scores are $0,3,7,9,11,13,15,17,21,27,29,31,33$: $13$ different scores.

**Answer: 13**

ukmt-sk-2017-10.title: Bound, then example
ukmt-sk-2017-10.body:
Let $A$ be a truther. It has exactly two liar neighbours and so one truther neighbour $B$. Then $B$, also a truther, has exactly two liar neighbours besides $A$. The four liars next to $A$ and $B$ are distinct, so there are at least $4$ liars and at most $4$ truthers.

Four is possible: let the truthers be $000,001,110,111$ (two opposite edges of the cube, vertices written as binary triples). Each truther has exactly one truther neighbour and two liar neighbours, so it tells the truth. Each liar, e.g. $010$, has neighbours $000$ (T), $011$ (L), $110$ (T), so exactly one liar neighbour; by symmetry every liar has exactly one liar neighbour, so its statement is false. The maximum is $4$.

**Answer: 4**

ukmt-sk-2017-11.title: Possible common differences
ukmt-sk-2017-11.body:
The common difference $d$ is a positive integer dividing $11-7=4$ (and $71-7=64$, $75-71=4$, etc.), so $d\in\{1,2,4\}$. The $100$th term is $7+99d$: $106$, $205$, $403$. Their sum is $714$.

**Answer: 714**

ukmt-sk-2017-12.title: Reflect and slide
ukmt-sk-2017-12.body:
Take each shaded half-ring that lies below the axis, reflect it in the axis and slide it $1$ cm to the left. The pieces then fit together into a single shaded semicircle of diameter $11$ cm. Its area is $\frac12\pi\left(\frac{11}2\right)^2=\frac{121}8\pi$, so $k=121$.

**Answer: 121**

ukmt-sk-2017-15.title: Case analysis
ukmt-sk-2017-15.body:
1 across is a two-digit square: $16,25,36,49,64,81$. 2 down is a three-digit number one less than a cube: $124,215,342,511,728,999$. The last digit of 1 across is the first digit of 2 down, so the possible pairs are $(25,511)$, $(49,999)$, $(81,124)$.

The first digit of 5 across equals the last digit of 2 down. For $(49,999)$ it would be $9$, but no two-digit square starts with $9$. For $(25,511)$, 5 across is $16$, 4 down ends in $6$ and 1 down starts with $2$ with $4\text{ down}-11=1\text{ down}$, giving $1\text{ down}=25$, $4\text{ down}=36$; but $\gcd(25,36)=1$, contradicting clue 4. For $(81,124)$, 5 across is $49$, 4 down ends in $9$ and starts... with $1\text{ down}$ starting with $8$: $88$ and $99$ work, and $\gcd(88,99)=11>1$. So all clues hold, and 3 across reads $8,2,9$: its digits are the second digit of 1 down ($8$), the second digit of 2 down ($2$) and the first digit of 4 down ($9$): $829$.

**Answer: 829**

ukmt-sk-2017-16.title: Lattice points and symmetry
ukmt-sk-2017-16.body:
The integer points on the circle of radius $5$ are $(\pm5,0),(0,\pm5),(\pm3,\pm4),(\pm4,\pm3)$: $12$ points. By symmetry the area is $4$ times the part in the first quadrant, which is split into two trapezia and a triangle: $\frac12(5+4)\cdot3+\frac12(4+3)\cdot1+\frac12\cdot3\cdot1=\frac{37}2$. So $\text{area}=4\times\frac{37}2=74$.

**Answer: 74**

ukmt-sk-2017-16.title: Shoelace for the quadrant
ukmt-sk-2017-16.body:
Points in the first quadrant in order: $(0,0),(5,0),(4,3),(3,4),(0,5)$. Shoelace: $\frac12|5\cdot3-4\cdot0+4\cdot4-3\cdot3+3\cdot5-0\cdot4|=\frac12(15+7+15)=\frac{37}2$. Multiply by $4$: $74$.

**Answer: 74**

ukmt-sk-2017-17.title: Filter the reversals
ukmt-sk-2017-17.body:
A reversed number ends in the first digit of the original square, so that first digit must be odd and not $5$: $1,3,7$ or $9$. The three-digit squares like this are $100,121,144,169,196,324,361,729,784,900,961$. Reversal keeps the digit sum, so squares divisible by $3$ ($144,324,729,900$) are out. The reversals of $100,121,169,961$ are $1$, $121$, $961$, $169$: not prime. The remaining squares $196,361,784$ reverse to $691,163,487$, all prime. Their mean is $\frac{691+163+487}{3}=447$.

**Answer: 447**

ukmt-sk-2017-18.title: Right triangles at the centre
ukmt-sk-2017-18.body:
Let $O$ be the midpoint of $PQ$, on diagonal $AC$ with $PQ\perp AC$ and $OP=10$. The angles of the rhombus at $A$ and $C$ are $120^\circ$ and $AC$ bisects them.

In right triangle $OPC$, $\angle OCP=60^\circ$, so $OC=\frac{10}{\tan60^\circ}=\frac{10}{\sqrt3}$. The distance from $O$ to side $AB$ is the radius $10$ (tangency) and $\angle OAB=60^\circ$, so $AO=\frac{10}{\sin60^\circ}=\frac{20}{\sqrt3}$. Therefore $AC=\frac{30}{\sqrt3}=10\sqrt3$.

Triangle $ABC$ has $AB=BC$ and $\angle ABC=60^\circ$, so it is equilateral and the side of the rhombus is $10\sqrt3$. The other diagonal is $BD=\sqrt3\cdot10\sqrt3=30$. The area is $\frac12\cdot10\sqrt3\cdot30=150\sqrt3$. So $a=150$, $b=3$ and $ab+a+b=450+150+3=603$.

**Answer: 603**

ukmt-sk-2017-19.title: Period three
ukmt-sk-2017-19.body:
$F_2=\frac1{1-x}$, $F_3=\frac1{1-\frac1{1-x}}=1-\frac1x$, $F_4=\frac1{1-(1-\frac1x)}=x$. So $F_{n+3}=F_n$ and $F_C=F_1=x$ exactly when $C\equiv1\pmod3$. The three-digit cubes are $125,216,343,512,729$, with remainders $2,0,1,2,0$ mod $3$. Only $343\equiv1$ works (for the others $F_C(C)$ is $\frac1{1-C}$ or $1-\frac1C\ne C$). The largest (indeed the only) possible value is $343$.

**Answer: 343**
